name: The royal-sage succession of the Gītā's yoga (BhG 4.1–3)

definitions.definition: The Lord taught the imperishable yoga to Vivasvat, Vivasvat to Manu, Manu to Ikṣvāku; the royal sages knew it through this succession (paramparā); over a long time it was lost, and the Lord teaches the same ancient yoga again to Arjuna because he is his devotee and friend, calling it the highest secret.

BhG 4.5–9: the Lord has passed through many births and knows them all; though unborn, imperishable and lord of beings, taking his stand on his own nature he comes into being by his own māyā; whenever dharma declines and adharma rises he sends himself forth, age after age, to protect the good, destroy wrongdoers and establish dharma; whoever knows his divine birth and action in truth is not reborn but comes to him. (The word 'avatāra' itself does not occur in these verses; the Gītā says 'I come into being', 'I send myself forth'.)

name: The Lord's reciprocity: as one approaches, so one is received (BhG 4.11)

definitions.definition: BhG 4.11: in whatever way people approach the Lord, in that way he receives them; humans follow his path in every way.

notes: Commentators read the second line either as all paths being finally the Lord's or as people following his example (cf. 3.23).

name: The varṇas by guṇa and action

definitions.definition: BhG 4.13: the fourfold class order (cāturvarṇya) was created by the Lord according to the division of guṇa and karma; though its maker, he is a non-doer. The verse does not say whether the division is fixed by birth or by conduct.

name: Non-doership (akartṛtva) in BhG 4–5

definitions.definition: BhG 4–5 teach non-doership on two sides. Of the Lord: though maker of the fourfold order he is to be known as a non-doer; actions do not stain him and he has no longing for their fruit, and whoever knows him thus is not bound (4.13–14). Of the knower: he sees inaction in action (4.18); abandoning attachment to fruit, though engaged in action he does nothing (4.20); knowing reality he thinks 'I do nothing', holding that the senses move among their objects (5.8–9); the embodied one sits in the city of nine gates neither acting nor causing action (5.13); the master does not create agency, actions or the link of action and fruit — nature acts; the all-pervading one takes no one's sin or merit (5.14–15).

notes: Whether 'prabhu'/'vibhu' in 5.14–15 is the Lord or the self is disputed by commentators.

definitions.definition: BhG 4.16–20: even the wise are bewildered about what action and inaction are; action, vikarma and inaction must each be understood, for the way of action is deep; whoever sees inaction in action and action in inaction is wise and yoked; the one free of attachment to fruit does nothing though fully engaged in action; the fire of knowledge burns all actions (4.37).

name: Action without attachment to its fruit (niṣkāma karma)

definitions.definition: BhG 4–6: undertakings free of desire and intention (4.19); abandoning attachment to the fruit, ever content, dependent on nothing (4.20); acting for the sake of sacrifice, action dissolves (4.23); acting with actions placed in Brahman, abandoning attachment, one is unstained like a lotus leaf (5.10); yogins act for self-purification (5.11); the yoked one abandons the fruit and gains peace, the unyoked is bound by attachment to it (5.12); the true renunciant and yogin does the required action without depending on its fruit (6.1).

name: The many forms of sacrifice (BhG 4.24–33)

definitions.definition: BhG 4.24–33 list the sacrifices offered by different practitioners, all born of action and all purifying: every element of the offering seen as Brahman; sacrifice to the gods; offering sacrifice by sacrifice into the fire of Brahman; offering the senses into the fires of restraint; offering sense objects into the fires of the senses; offering the activities of the senses and of breath into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint; sacrifice with material things, with austerity, with yoga, with study and with knowledge; offering prāṇa into apāna and apāna into prāṇa, with breath-regulation; offering the breaths into the breaths with regulated food. The sacrifice of knowledge is the best, since all action culminates in knowledge.

members: offering sacrifice into the fire of Brahman (4.25)
senses into the fires of restraint (4.26)
sense objects into the fires of the senses (4.26)
activities of senses and breath into the fire of ātma-saṃyama-yoga (4.27)
prāṇa into apāna, apāna into prāṇa; prāṇāyāma (4.29)
breaths into breaths with regulated food (4.30)

relations.note: most members carry the fire-offering over to inner disciplines

definitions.definition: BhG 4.25–30 carries the language of the fire-offering over to inner disciplines: the senses offered into the fires of restraint, sense objects into the fires of the senses, the activities of senses and breath into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint kindled by knowledge, prāṇa into apāna and apāna into prāṇa.

BhG 5.4–5: the childish, not the learned, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as separate; one properly established in either obtains the fruit of both; the place reached by the followers of Sāṃkhya is reached by those of Yoga too, and whoever sees them as one truly sees. In context Sāṃkhya is aligned with renunciation, Yoga with the yoga of action; 6.2 likewise says that what is called renunciation is yoga.

BhG 5–6 define renunciation inwardly: the constant renunciant is one who neither hates nor desires (5.3); all actions are renounced with the mind (5.13); the renunciant is the one who does the required action without depending on its fruit, not one who merely has no sacred fire and no rites (6.1); no one becomes a yogin without renouncing intention (6.2). Renunciation of action and the yoga of action both lead to the highest good, the latter being superior, and renunciation is hard to attain without yoga (5.2, 5.6).

BhG 4–6 repeatedly describe the one established in yoga as seeing the same: the same in success and failure (4.22); seeing all beings in the self and then in the Lord (4.35); seeing the same in a learned brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste (5.18); the mind established in sameness is established in Brahman, which is the same (5.19); clod, stone and gold the same (6.8); an equal mind toward friend and foe, good and wicked (6.9); seeing the self in all beings and all beings in the self (6.29); seeing the Lord everywhere and everything in him (6.30); seeing pleasure and pain everywhere by likeness to oneself (6.32).

BhG 5.24–26 name the goal brahma-nirvāṇa: the yogin with happiness, delight and light within, having become Brahman, attains it; seers whose stains are destroyed, whose doubts are cut, self-restrained and delighting in the welfare of all beings, attain it; for ascetics free of desire and anger, of restrained mind, who know the self, it is present all around. 6.15 speaks of the peace culminating in nirvāṇa that abides in the Lord.

name: The self as its own friend and enemy (BhG 6.5–6)

definitions.definition: BhG 6.5–6: one should raise the self by the self and not let it sink; the self alone is the self's friend and the self alone its enemy — friend to the one who has conquered himself, while for the one not self-possessed the self acts with hostility like an enemy.

name: The fate of the one fallen from yoga

definitions.definition: BhG 6.37–45: asked whether the faithful but insufficiently striving one whose mind falls from yoga perishes like a scattered cloud, the Lord answers that there is no destruction for him here or hereafter, since no doer of good goes to a bad end: he reaches the worlds of the meritorious, dwells there long and is born in a pure and prosperous house, or — rarer — in a family of wise yogins; there he regains his former understanding and strives again, carried on by former practice even against his will; even the inquirer into yoga passes beyond the word-Brahman; striving with effort, cleansed, perfected over many births, the yogin reaches the highest goal.

BhG 5.20 describes the knower of Brahman in the same terms as the steady-wise of 2.54–72: not elated by the pleasant nor agitated by the unpleasant, steady in intellect (sthira-buddhi), undeluded, established in Brahman.

BhG 4–6 (the Lord speaking of himself): unborn, imperishable, lord of beings, coming into being by his own māyā (4.6); maker of the fourfold order yet non-doer, unstained by action, without longing for fruit (4.13–14); enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, great lord of all worlds, friend of all beings (5.29); seen everywhere and holding everything in himself, never lost to the one who sees thus (6.30); abiding in all beings (6.31); the object of the meditator's thought and the goal of peace (6.14–15).

BhG 4–6: the Lord and Arjuna have had many births (4.5); knowing the Lord's divine birth and action frees one from rebirth (4.9); those intent on That reach non-return (5.17); the one fallen from yoga is reborn after dwelling in the worlds of the meritorious and regains the understanding of his former body (6.41–43); the yogin is perfected over many births (6.45).
